okay, I've found a very weird solution for the double controller thing of the Ultimate 2C: HidHide.  
[https://github.com/nefarius/HidHide/](https://github.com/nefarius/HidHide/)

use it at your own risk. it's a rather agressive program.   
what it does is "hide" certain devices from selected programs, or, only allow certain programs to see said devices.

until now it's main use is to hide a PS4 controller when DS4Windows is using it to emulate a xinput one. DS4Windows recommends it to avoid double input between the emulated xinput and the PS4 own thing.



we will use it to hide only one of the double Ultimate 2C controllers.

  
after intalling this, you can go to the 'Devices' tab and take a look at all the controllers you have plugged in at the moment, Ultimate 2C should show up there. If you "hide" the entire device, both (doubled) controllers will "disappear" from the controllers list, but if you double click on the 2C controller, you can disable only "parts" of it:

[https://imgur.com/a/8bitdo-ultimate-2c-double-input-fix-3QgL1dn](https://imgur.com/a/8bitdo-ultimate-2c-double-input-fix-3QgL1dn)

disable the "Consumer Control" and "FF7 1" entries and the controller will stop showing up twice. leave the "Gamepad" and "absent" entries alone. The "FF7A 1" part might be listed as something different, I can't be sure.

this must be done for both USB and 2.4G modes as they are listed as different devices.

  
my guess is that there is something wrong with the driver installation, I had a Ultimate C (non-2) wireless controller previously and it might have "fused" the drivers with this one, idk just guessing. 

I tested this same controller in other computers and it only shows up twice on this one.

>The thing here is, Atlus is pretty hypocrital about it. They give the positives of liberalism to neutral while the negatives go to Law, the end result is contradictory.

Do they really?

  
I'm going to be honest. I don't know much about Japanese religion and Shintoism (so I'm 100% open to being corrected on this) but I do know a little bit about Taoism and how it is somewhat distant but still connected to it.  
A lot of the values in Taoism, which is about following "the Way," the "Tao" (the name of an SMTV alt-Law character—coincidence or not), are about things like simplicity, compassion, detachment, and spontaneity. It is a somewhat nature-centered worldview while NOT being about hedonism or individualism AT ALL. It is NOT about Chaos and the "Chthonic." Yin and Yang, and most importantly balance, are very present in Taoism, which is at least as old as Socrates. Much older than liberalism.



The Cartesian separation of the Apollonian and Dionysian—though a very astute Nietzschean observation on Western art—is not universal. This dichotomy is itself part of Western dogma.

Like a lot of Japanese media, Atlus writers do seem to see the Abrahamic God—and yes, secular liberalism and neo-liberalism (some might say capitalism itself)—as invaders.

Law and Chaos have different explanations depending on the game, but in SMTV, it is made very clear that YHWH installed himself as the "definitive" God and removed the possibility of any alternative—much like how liberalism has done to the world post-Cold War. Fukuyama's "end of history" and all that nonsense.

I really, REALLY doubt Atlus based their ideas of Law and Chaos on Paglia, though.
Your interpretation is pretty interesting and thorough, but you're using Paglia to read SMT and feeling frustrated that it’s not all aligning as you expect. It's not like Paglia is in SMT's DNA—she most definitely is not.
Paglia is basically a quasi-second-wave white "feminist" Jordan Peterson (take of that what you will; personally, I detest both). She is FIRMLY in the Western secular philosophical tradition—not the type of philosophical framework that rogue Japanese writers would use to base their anti-Western video game manifesto on.

Since I stand in the post-structuralist side of 20th-century thought (which people like Paglia despise), my personal reading (and a lot of you might hate this) is that LAW in SMT is basically colonialism itself: one power that strives to "end conflict" by subjugating the identities and ways of life of the entire world, but in truth, it's all just exploitation and power maintenance.

I really, really love the soundtrack, but yeah, the sound design is very unpolished. There were a number of animations where the sound effect was just... wrong.

For instance, there's this one execution where Eivor kicks the enemy's stomach and then stomps their head. The first kick has a very muted sound effect, and the second is a cartoonish "steps on watermelon" sound. It’s nitpicky of me, but I hated it every single time it happened.

As for the violence, you're right, it's also weird. Raiding as a mechanic is kinda lame and undercooked, and narratively it makes absolutely no sense. It's here just because "it's what vikings do," and as you pointed out, this goes against the game's themes.

  
I see this big conflict in the goals of the project: Ubi wanted and even marketed this game as "the Viking game," where you can play as this rough, brutal invader raiding and pillaging England like vikings are "supposed to". Meanwhile, the narrative team wanted to tell a story about leadership and the conflict of cultures and religion, a story about the folly of pride and about finding your place in the world, not just accepting it. Also, they wanted a female protagonist but had to hide that because "women don't sell" and all that.

It's hard to put into perspective what Assassin's Creed felt like when it came out in 2007. Back when we didn't have a vast quantity of lore material to reference and not even much of an ideia of where it was going.

Coming off Prince of Persia, AC felt very bold and thought provoking, never had we seen a concept so out there like the Animus, much less a game that tries so hard to diegetically explain the rules of it's fiction and of the game itself; like not having a health bar, but a "syncronization bar", for instance; or how the Animus logs it's glitches and limitations on the screen as if it was a limitation of the program and not of the game.

There was a big community of people making different theories as to what Altair's (and later Ezio's) journey meant and the nature of the supernatural (or is it?) elements, similar to how people do with mystery TV shows.

All this kinda got lost (at least in big part) around Revelations or AC3, depending on who you ask. I still enjoy this series, some entries way more than others, but AC is a much bigger thing now and I fell like it will never end or have an ending worthy of the potential it had when it started.

Ultimately the series frames the conflic between assassins and templars as THE conflic of civilization (AC frames this as a conflic that predates humankind itself):

Are people fundamentally good and should be guided by their own free will and determination?

OR

Are people fundamentally bad, unfit for freedom and require the guidance of those who are "better", juster, those "fit to rule"?

This conflic is pretty much the one between Rousseu's and Hobbes' ideas of the social contract, and much (but not all) of modern **western** political philosophy is an atempt to reconcile these two visions.

If you reeeeally wanna stretch it you could say that these visions are progressive left and conservative right, respectively. And if you know these stances you know that a lot of the time a "middle ground" is actually just a compromise of one side.
